title: Balls, Races, Water, Ice
bigQuestion: Why do ball games, races, swimming and ice games each need their own place?

story.title: The Floor Changes
story.kicker: A class walks outside and feels the ground change under their shoes.
paragraphs: A second-grade class lines up in the gym. The floor is smooth wood. Two hoops hang high at each end. Every step squeaks a little.
The class walks out the side door. Now the ground is soft grass. White lines mark a long rectangle. A goal net stands at each end.
Past the grass is an oval of red rubber. It has lanes painted in white. A boy taps it with his shoe. It feels springy, not soft.
Back inside, the teacher asks a question. Could you swim on the grass? Could you skate on the wood? Each kind of play needs its own ground.
story.think: What is the ground like in each play place at your school?

lessons.title: Races at Olympia
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, people in Greece ran races in a stadium at Olympia.
reading: *Olympia* is a place in Greece. Games were held there long ago. The traditional date for the first games is 776 BCE. They came every four years.
A main race was one length of the *stadium*. The stadium was a long, straight dirt track. People sat on grassy banks beside it to watch.

words.d: the place in Greece where the ancient Olympic Games were held
a long place built for races, with room for people to watch

look.title: Two Race Paths
look.text: Look at a long, straight dirt path at old Olympia. Grass banks rise on each side. Now look at a modern red oval with eight white lanes. Both were built so a race has a place.
look.prompt: What is the same about these two paths? What is different?

check.q: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held?
check.why: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia, a place in Greece.

check.q: What was the old stadium at Olympia like?
check.why: The stadium was a long, straight dirt track for races.

check.q: Where did people sit to watch?
choices: on wood seats in a gym
check.why: People sat on grassy banks beside the stadium.

lessons.title: Stone Courts for a Rubber Ball
lessons.mainIdea: People in ancient Mexico and Central America built stone courts for a ball game.
reading: People in Mexico and Central America played a ball game long ago. It began more than 3,000 years ago. The ball was made of *rubber* from trees.
Players needed a special place. They built a *ball court* of stone. It was a long, narrow alley. High walls stood on both sides. The largest one is at Chichén Itzá in Mexico.

words.d: a bouncy material made from the sap of certain trees
a long stone alley with walls, built for the ancient Mesoamerican ball game

look.title: The Great Ball Court
look.text: Look at a long grass alley at Chichén Itzá. Tall stone walls rise on each side. High on each wall is a stone ring. People built this court more than 800 years ago.
look.prompt: Why would a ball game need walls instead of an open field?

check.q: What was the old ball made of?
check.why: The Mesoamerican ball was made of rubber from tree sap.

check.q: What did players build for this game?
check.why: They built long stone ball courts with walls.

check.q: Where is the largest old ball court?
check.why: The largest ancient ball court is at Chichén Itzá in Mexico.

lessons.title: A Pitch for Soccer
lessons.mainIdea: Soccer clubs in London wrote shared rules in 1863, and the game is played on a pitch.
reading: In 1863, clubs in London met at a tavern. They wrote shared rules for a kicking game. They named their group the *Football Association*.
Their game is called soccer in the United States. It is played on a *pitch*. A pitch is a long rectangle of grass or turf. A goal stands at each end.

words.d: the group of English clubs that wrote shared soccer rules in 1863
the grass or turf rectangle where soccer is played

look.title: The Meeting in 1863
look.text: On 26 October 1863, football clubs met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. They formed the Football Association. They wanted teams from different places to play by the same rules.
look.cite: The Football Association, record of its founding meeting, Freemasons' Tavern, London, 26 October 1863
look.prompt: Why would teams from different places want the same rules?

check.q: When did London clubs form the Football Association?
check.why: The Football Association was formed in London in 1863.

check.q: What is a pitch?
check.why: A pitch is the grass or turf rectangle where soccer is played.

check.q: Where did the clubs meet?
check.why: They met at the Freemasons' Tavern in London.

lessons.title: A Game Made for a Gym
lessons.mainIdea: James Naismith made basketball for a gym in Springfield, Massachusetts, in 1891.
reading: *James Naismith* taught at a school in Springfield, Massachusetts. In December 1891, winter kept his class inside. The students were bored and restless.
Naismith needed a game that fit a *gym*. He nailed two peach baskets to the balcony. Players tossed a soccer ball at them. That game became basketball.

words.d: the teacher who made up basketball in 1891
a big indoor room with a hard floor, built for games and exercise

look.title: Naismith's Winter Class
look.text: Naismith wrote that his class at the YMCA training school needed an indoor game for the winter of 1891. He used a soccer ball and two peach baskets.
look.cite: James Naismith, Basketball: Its Origin and Development (1941)
look.prompt: Why did the season matter to where the game was played?

check.q: Why did Naismith need an indoor game?
check.why: In December 1891, winter kept his class inside.

check.q: What did Naismith nail to the balcony?
check.why: He nailed two peach baskets to the balcony.

check.q: In what town did basketball begin?
check.why: Naismith taught in Springfield, Massachusetts.

lessons.title: A Lap of 400 Meters
lessons.mainIdea: One lap in the inside lane of a standard outdoor track is 400 meters.
reading: A modern running *track* is an oval. It has painted *lanes*. Each runner stays in one lane. Lanes keep runners from bumping.
One lap in the inside lane is 400 meters. World Athletics sets that size. Tracks around the world match it. So a time in one town can be compared with another.

words.d: an oval path with lanes, built for running races
a marked strip that one runner stays in during a race

look.title: Race Lengths on a Track
look.cite: World Athletics, Competition and Technical Rules: 100 m race; 200 m standard indoor track; 400 m standard outdoor track
look.prompt: Which is longer, one lap indoors or one lap outdoors?

check.q: How long is one outdoor lap in the inside lane?
check.why: A standard outdoor track is 400 meters in the inside lane.

check.q: Why do tracks match in size?
choices: so they fit in a gym
check.why: Same-size tracks let a time in one town be compared with another.

check.q: What is a lane?
choices: a strip one runner stays in
check.why: A lane is the marked strip one runner stays in.

lessons.title: A Pool Has Walls
lessons.mainIdea: Swim races need a pool with a measured length from wall to wall.
reading: Swimmers race in a *pool*. A pool is a tank of water with walls. Its length is measured. Swimmers touch the wall at each end.
Many school pools in the United States are 25 yards long. The Olympic Games use a longer pool. It is 50 meters from wall to wall.

words.d: a tank of water with walls, measured for swim races

look.title: Two Pools
look.text: Look at a school pool. It is 25 yards long. A swimmer touches the far wall quickly. Now look at an Olympic pool. It is 50 meters long. The far wall looks much farther away.
look.prompt: Which pool would take longer to swim across? How do you know?

check.q: How long are many U.S. school pools?
check.why: Many U.S. school pools are 25 yards long.

check.q: How long is an Olympic pool?
check.why: The Olympic Games use a pool 50 meters long.

check.q: What do swimmers touch at each end?
check.why: A pool has walls, and swimmers touch the wall at each end.

lessons.title: Ice Needs a Rink
lessons.mainIdea: Ice hockey moved indoors to a rink, and an NHL rink is 200 feet long.
reading: Hockey is played on ice. People once played on frozen ponds. In 1875, a game was played indoors in Montreal, Canada. It was at the Victoria Skating *Rink*.
A rink is a floor of ice with walls around it. Today a *National Hockey League* rink is 200 feet long. It is 85 feet wide. The corners are curved.

words.d: a floor of ice with walls around it, used for hockey and skating
the top professional hockey league in the United States and Canada, called the NHL

look.title: An NHL Rink
look.cite: National Hockey League, Official Rules, Rule 1 (Rink): 200 feet by 85 feet, corners rounded in the arc of a circle with a radius of 28 feet
look.prompt: Which is bigger, the length or the width?

check.q: Where did people play hockey before indoor rinks?
check.why: People once played hockey on frozen ponds.

check.q: Where was an indoor game played in 1875?
check.why: In 1875 a game was played at the Victoria Skating Rink in Montreal.

check.q: How long is an NHL rink?
check.why: An NHL rink is 200 feet long and 85 feet wide.

review.q: Where did people run races in a stadium long ago?
review.why: The ancient Olympic Games were held at Olympia in Greece.

review.q: What did ancient players in Mexico build for their ball game?
review.why: They built long stone ball courts with high walls.

review.q: What group wrote soccer rules in London in 1863?
review.why: London clubs formed the Football Association in 1863.

review.q: Why did Naismith make a game for a gym?
review.why: In December 1891 winter kept his class indoors.
One lap in the inside lane of an outdoor track is 400 meters.

review.q: Which place has walls that swimmers touch?
review.why: A pool is a tank of water with walls at each end.
